A test is only useful if its error rate is what it claims. When spiDE reports
a $q$-value below 0.05, the expected share of false calls among the calls
should be at most 5%. This vignette shows how that was checked on real spatial
data and on simulated data with a known truth, and what the checks found. It
is the one place in the package that quotes these numbers. The full studies
behind them are published on the
[spiDE research site](https://bhuvalab.github.io/spiDE-research/).

# How calibration is checked

The idea is to run spiDE on data where, by construction, there is nothing to
find, and see whether it stays quiet. Two such *null* data sets are made from
each real cohort:

- **The block null** (the neighbourhood is scrambled). In every tissue
  section the niche densities are shifted by a random offset, wrapping around
  the edges, so each cell is given the neighbourhood of a cell elsewhere in
  the same section. The niche maps stay as smooth as real ones, but a cell's
  expression no longer has anything to do with its neighbourhood. Both the
  pooled and the condition-specific test should find nothing. Each shifted
  map is a full refit.
- **The permutation null** (the condition is scrambled). The condition labels
  are shuffled between patients, within each slide so that a slide difference
  cannot pose as a condition difference. The niche effects are real, but they
  no longer differ between the shuffled groups, so the condition-specific
  test should find nothing.

On each null, two things are read:

| reading | what it means | pass |
|---|---|---|
| **spread** | For every gene, the root-mean-square of its null $z$-statistics; the median over genes, in each fifth of genes by expression. A calibrated test gives 1. | 0.90 to 1.10 in every fifth |
| **tail** | The fraction of null data sets in which a Benjamini-Hochberg screen at 0.05 made at least one call. | at most 0.10 (block), 0.07 (permutation) |

Spread checks the whole distribution of the test statistics, not only the
extreme ones. The tail checks the extreme ones, which are what become calls.

# The cohorts

| cohort | platform, tissue | condition (patients) | bandwidth |
|---|---|---|---|
| GSE250346 | Xenium, lung (pulmonary fibrosis) | control 9, disease 26 | 60 µm |
| GSE282639 | CosMx 1k, lung (IPF) | control 13, IPF 15 | 30 µm |
| GSE289194 | CosMx 1k, lymph node | extranodal 20, nodal 24 | 30 µm |
| YTMA | CosMx WTA, NSCLC | non-responder 30, responder 25 | 30 µm |
| YTMA stage | CosMx WTA, lung adenocarcinoma | early 123, late 40 | 30 µm |

Each cohort was analysed in its five best-covered cell types, as both index
and niche types, with every other cell adjusted for as one further niche. The
three public cohorts carry the conclusions below. The two YTMA cohorts are
shown for completeness.

# The slopes engine (the default)

Ten block-null maps and 1,000 condition permutations per cohort:

| cohort | pooled, block: spread (tail) | condition, block: spread (tail) | condition, permutation: spread | tail, all / filtered |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GSE250346 | 0.94-0.96 (0) | 0.95-0.96 (0) | 0.98-0.99 | 0 / 0.010 |
| GSE282639 | 0.92-0.96 (0) | 0.97-1.00 (0) | 0.99-1.00 | 0.015 / 0.042 |
| GSE289194 | 0.93-0.95 (0) | 0.97-0.99 (0) | 0.99 | 0.015 / 0.027 |
| YTMA | 0.93-0.94 (0) | 0.98 (0) | 0.99 | 0.010 / 0.035 |
| YTMA stage | 0.96-0.97 (0) | 0.98 (0) | 0.99 | 0.012 / 0.023 |

Every criterion is met in every cohort. The spread sits slightly below 1 for
the pooled test, so its $p$-values are, if anything, a little conservative.
"Filtered" is the default procedure (the condition-specific test among the
triplets that pass the pooled test) and "all" tests every triplet.

# The sandwich engine

The same nulls, with 50 permutations per cohort, because each permutation of
the sandwich engine is a refit:

| cohort | pooled, block: spread (tail) | condition, block: spread (tail) | condition, permutation: spread | tail, all / filtered |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GSE250346 | 0.97-1.01 (0) | 0.93-0.98 (0) | 1.00-1.02 | 0 / 0 |
| GSE282639 | 0.99-1.01 (0) | 0.96-0.99 (0) | 1.01-1.04 | 0.02 / 0 |
| GSE289194 | 1.03-1.06 (0) | 1.03-1.06 (0) | 1.06-1.10 | 0.02 / 0.06 |
| YTMA | 0.99-1.00 (0) | 0.99-1.00 (0) | 1.00-1.02 | 0.04 / 0.14 |
| YTMA stage | 1.00-1.01 (0.20) | 0.99-1.00 (0) | 1.00-1.02 | 0 / 0 |

On the stage cohort (163 patients) a sandwich permutation is a refit of about an hour, so its
permutation null has 40 permutations. The sandwich engine runs closer to a spread of 1 but less evenly. It reaches
1.10 on GSE289194, its filtered procedure called in 7 of 50 permutations on
YTMA, and it called in 2 of 10 block maps on the stage cohort. It is a useful
second opinion; the slopes engine is the one to rely on.

# Accuracy and power, with a known truth

Real data cannot tell how large an effect truly is, or which calls are true.
For that, counts were simulated from models fitted to four of these cohorts
(their real cell positions, cell types, patients and niche maps, with
gene-specific library-size effects that vary across the tissue). Condition by
niche effects were then planted, either shared by all patients or varying
between them. Six ways in which sequencing depth can relate to the niche were
simulated, with 20 data sets per scenario, on GSE289194 and YTMA: the two cohorts
whose simulations passed a check of realism against their real data (library
sizes, detection, dispersion and the genes' response to depth). The
simulations of GSE282639 and GSE250346 failed that check and were run on two
of the six scenarios, as a description only.

For the condition-specific test (filtered procedure), averaged over data sets:

| template | engine | relative bias of the estimate (worst depth scenario) | coverage of 95% intervals | true-positive rate | false discovery proportion |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GSE289194 | slopes | -0.03 (0.06) | 0.90 | 0.57 | 0.041 |
| GSE289194 | sandwich | -0.02 (0.05) | 0.88 | 0.23 | 0.047 |
| YTMA | slopes | -0.03 (0.05) | 0.94 | 0.28 | 0.032 |
| YTMA | sandwich | -0.01 (0.02) | 0.92 | 0.21 | 0.047 |

- **Estimates are close to the truth.** On average they are within about 3%
  of the planted effect, and within about 6% in the worst depth scenario.
- **The slopes engine finds more true effects:** about 2.5 times as many as
  the sandwich engine on GSE289194. The gain is largest when effects vary
  between patients.
- **Both keep the false discovery proportion below 5%.** On the two
  simulations that failed the realism check, the slopes engine's filtered
  procedure ran higher (0.05 on GSE282639 and 0.12 on GSE250346). Those
  simulations do not resemble their real data closely enough to say whether
  this carries over to real data; the real-data nulls above show no excess.

The pooled test found 26% of the planted pooled effects on GSE289194 and 3% on
YTMA with the slopes engine (14% and 5% with the sandwich engine); on YTMA the
effects were small against the count noise of whole-transcriptome data.

# How much data is needed

A separate benchmark measured how recall and false discoveries change with the
design. It used the same four simulated tissues, the shipped slopes engine and
1,020 simulated datasets. The design varied:

- the number of patients, 6 to 32, half per condition;
- the cells per patient and index type, 25 to 1,000;
- the gene panel.

Every dataset carried planted niche effects of six sizes on known genes. A
size is a *standardised slope*: a log fold change per within-patient standard
deviation of the log1p niche density. A slope of 0.2 is about a 1.6-fold
change between index cells at the niche's 10th and 90th percentiles; 0.4 is
about 2.7-fold. On the three public cohorts the median pooled call is 0.07 to 0.14.

The smallest effect the pooled test finds with 80% recall at BH 0.05, at 200
cells per patient and index type:

| patients | GSE289194 | GSE282639 | GSE250346 | YTMA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | > 0.8 | > 0.8 | > 0.8 | > 0.8 |
| 12 | > 0.8 | 0.65 | 0.77 | > 0.8 |
| 16 | 0.65 | 0.45 | 0.58 | > 0.8 |
| 24 | 0.41 | 0.32 | 0.35 | 0.63 |
| 32 | 0.32 | 0.26 | 0.31 | 0.43 |
| 32, with 1,000 cells | 0.19 | 0.18 | 0.17 | 0.44 |

- **Patients set the power.**
  - For a fixed number of cells, dividing them among more patients did better
    in all but 5 of 528 comparisons, none of them beyond noise. At 3,200 cells
    per type on GSE289194, 8 patients found 2% of effects of 0.4, 16 patients
    50% and 32 patients 84%.
  - Below 12 patients, neither test calls anything but very large effects.
  - With 3 patients per condition, the condition-specific test cannot run.
- **Cells help once patients are adequate.** At 32 patients, recall of effects
  of 0.2 on GSE289194 rose from 0.59 at 200 cells to 0.84 at 1,000.
- **The condition-specific test needs larger effects.** Take the test over all
  triplets, for an effect present in one condition only. Where both tests
  reach 80% recall, it needs 2.2 to 3.0 times the pooled test's effect. This
  is a lower bound: the condition test reaches 80% in fewer designs.
  - The default filtered procedure cannot find an effect that reverses between
    the conditions, since such an effect has no mean slope.
  - `procedure = "all"` found as many condition effects or more at 98% of
    design points.
- **Dim genes are found last.** Recall rises steadily with the gene's
  expression in the index type.
- **False discoveries.**
  - The false discovery proportion stayed within its nominal level across most
    designs. The all-null datasets gave almost no calls at any size, up to
    1,000 cells and 32 patients.
  - It ran above nominal in the most precise designs, above all on the 343-gene
    panel of GSE250346 (up to 0.31 at a nominal 0.05). On the 1,000-gene panels
    the excess appeared only at 32 patients with 400 to 1,000 cells (up to 0.14).
  - The measurements point to a compositional cause. Strong niche effects in
    bright genes move the library size with the niche, and relative to the
    library every other gene in that (index, niche) column then moves the
    other way. Those changes are real changes in a gene's share of the counts,
    but they are not niche effects on the gene itself.
  - If many weak calls share one column and one sign, check that column's
    median slope and the library size against the niche.

The full results, with an interactive planner over patients, cells and effect
size, are in
[How much data does spiDE need?](https://bhuvalab.github.io/spiDE-research/power-results.html).
The simulation design is in
[Simulating realistic spatial data](https://bhuvalab.github.io/spiDE-research/power-design.html).

# Sequencing depth

A cell's library size mixes technical capture with its biological RNA
content, and the RNA content can itself depend on the neighbourhood. Depth
handling was therefore judged by how accurately each option recovered the
planted effects, not by how much library-size signal it removed. Four options
were compared in the simulations above:

- one slope on the log library size (`depth = "loglib"`);
- a smooth curve in it (`"nonlinear"`);
- a library-size effect that varies across the tissue (`"spatial_spline"`);
- SpaNorm's library-size component as a fixed offset.

In the slopes engine the four lay within 0.015 of each other in bias, with the
same power, and every one was calibrated in every scenario, so the default is
the simplest, `"loglib"`. (The sandwich engine with `"loglib"` ran wide on
GSE289194, up to 1.13.) The spatial option costs a median of 1.2 to 1.8 times
as much to fit, per template, in the slopes engine.

One consequence holds for every option. When the neighbourhood raises a cell's
total RNA, adjusting for library size also removes that part of the niche
effect, so a pooled slope reports expression **relative to the cell's total
RNA**. In the simulations this removed most of a niche-driven change in total
RNA from the pooled slope. The condition-specific test is affected only by the
part of that change that differs between conditions.

# Gene sets

`spiGSEA()` was checked the same way, on about 6,400 GO biological-process
sets per cohort (10 to 500 genes each), with 20 block maps and 200 condition
permutations:

| cohort | pooled, block: spread (tail) | condition, block: spread (tail) | condition, permutation: spread (tail) |
|---|---|---|---|
| GSE250346 | 0.91-0.98 (0) | 0.96 (0) | 0.97-0.98 (0) |
| GSE282639 | 0.90-1.00 (0) | 0.97-0.98 (0) | 0.99-1.00 (0.005) |
| GSE289194 | 0.96-1.00 (0) | 0.97 (0) | 0.99 (0.005) |
| YTMA | 0.98-1.00 (0) | 0.97-0.98 (0) | 0.99 (0.015) |
| YTMA stage | 1.03-1.05 (0.05) | 0.97 (0) | 0.99 (0.010) |

Spread is read per fifth of sets by size, and a tail counts a call at
`q.global` < 0.05. The set tests are calibrated in every cohort.

# The between-patient test

`testNicheAbundance()` was checked with 200 permutations within slide per
cohort, each of two kinds:

- **condition permutations:** the condition labels shuffled across patients,
  the null of the term `"condition:niche"`;
- **niche permutations:** each patient's niche abundances shuffled across
  patients, the null of the term `"niche"`.

The tail is the share of permutations with any call at `q.global` < 0.05,
against a limit of 0.07:

| cohort | condition:niche, no cap | condition:niche, default cap | niche, no cap | niche, default cap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GSE250346 | 0.15 | 0.050 | 0.15 | 0.010 |
| GSE282639 | 0.03 | 0.025 | 0.07 | 0.055 |
| GSE289194 | 0.07 | 0.040 | 0.14 | 0.075 |
| YTMA | 0.07 | 0.025 | 0.145 | 0.060 |
| YTMA stage | 0.28 | 0.010 | 0.33 | 0.020 |

- **Without the leverage cap**, a single patient at the edge of a niche type's
  abundances made false calls in up to a third of permutations.
- **The default, `max.leverage = 3`,** is the weakest cap that keeps the
  condition test within its limit on all three public cohorts. A cap of 2
  over-corrects: its null spread falls to 0.56-0.68.
- **At the default the test is slightly conservative** on GSE250346 (spread
  0.86-0.95) and YTMA stage (0.86-0.88), and calibrated on the other three
  (0.93-1.02).
- **A finer design breaks it.** On the YTMA cohort split into 13 or 24 cell
  types, with many types that have only 14-36 cells per patient, the condition
  test still made false calls in 11-35% of permutations at the default cap. Its
  calls are not reliable when each patient contributes few cells of the index
  type.

# What has not been measured

- **Bandwidth.** Each cohort was checked at one bandwidth. Comparing results
  across bandwidths is a sensitivity analysis, and each bandwidth is its own
  set of tests.
- **Many index types at once on small panels.** The checks used five index
  types per cohort. With many more, the pooled test's multiple-testing burden
  grows and power falls accordingly; calibration is not expected to change.
- **Very small cohorts on real data.** The smallest real group checked had 9
  patients. The power benchmark above simulated cohorts down to 6 patients
  (3 per condition).
  - There the pooled test is conservative: the spread of its null statistics is
    0.83 to 0.88, against 1 for a calibrated test.
  - The condition-specific test cannot run, because it needs at least 3
    effective patients per condition.
